267 "Mater Alchimia" could serve as the name of a whole epoch. 
Beginning, roughly, with Christianity, it gave birth in the six­
teenth and seventeenth centuries to the age of science, only to 
perish, unrecognized and misunderstood, and sink from sight in 
the stream of the centuries as an age that had been outlived. But, 
just as every mother was once a daughter, so too was alchemy. 
It owes its real beginnings to the Gnostic systems, which Hip-
polytus rightly regarded as philosophic, and which, with the 
help of Greek philosophy and the mythologies of the Near and 
Middle East, together with Christian dogmatics and Jewish 
cabalism, made extremely interesting attempts, from the mod­
ern point of view, to synthetize a unitary vision of the world in 
which the physical and the mystical aspects played equal parts. 
Had this attempt succeeded, we would not be witnessing today 
the curious spectacle of two parallel world-views neither of 
which knows, or wishes to know, anything about the other. 
Hippolytus was in the enviable position of being able to see 
Christian doctrine side by side with its pagan sisters, and similar 
comparisons had also been attempted by Justin Martyr. To the 
honour of Christian thinking it must be said that up till the 
time of Kepler there was no lack of praiseworthy attempts to 
interpret and understand Nature, in the broadest sense, on the 
basis of Christian dogma. 
68 These attempts, however, inevitably came to grief for lack 
of any adequate knowledge of natural processes. Thus, in the 
course of the eighteenth century, there arose that notorious rift 
between faith and knowledge. Faith lacked experience and sci­
ence missed out the soul. Instead, science believed fervently in 
absolute objectivity and assiduously overlooked the fundamental 
difficulty that the real vehicle and begetter of all knowledge is 
the psyche, the very thing that scientists knew the least about

represents and personifies the dark and unfathomable, the 
watery deep, the forest, the night, the cave. When a primitive 
says "snake," he means an experience of something extrahuman. 
The snake is not an allegory or metaphor, for its own peculiar 
form is symbolic in itself, and it is essential to note that the 
"Son" has the form of a snake and not the other way round: the 
snake does not signify the "Son."

295 All three symbols are phenomena of assimilation that are in

make it quite obvious what is meant: the greater, more com­

well-known symbol for God; and so (in a certain sense) is the 
cross, the quaternity in all its forms, e.g., Ezekiel's vision, the 
Rex gloriae with the four evangelists, the Gnostic Barbelo 
("God in four") and Kolorbas ("all four"); the duality (tao, 
hermaphrodite, father-mother); and finally, the human form 
(child, son, anthropos) and the individual personality (Christ 
and Buddha), to name only the most important of the motifs 
here used. 
i°5 All these images are found, empirically, to be expressions for 
the unified wholeness of man. The fact that this goal goes by the 
name of "God" proves that it has a numinous character; and in­
deed, experiences, dreams, and visions of this kind do have a 
fascinating and impressive quality which can be spontaneously 
felt even by people who are not prejudiced in their favour by 
prior psychological knowledge. So it is no wonder that na'ive 
minds make no distinction between God and the image they 
have experienced. Wherever, therefore, we find symbols indica­
tive of psychic wholeness, we encounter the na'ive idea that they 
stand for God. In the case of those quite common Romanesque 
pictures of the Son of Man accompanied by three angels with 
animal heads and one with a human head, for example, it would 
be simpler to assume that the Son of Man meant the ordinary 
man and that the problem of one against three referred to the 
well-known psychological schema of one differentiated and 
three undifferentiated functions. But this interpretation would,

354 The inhabitant of the quadratic space leads to the human 
figure. Apart from the geometrical and arithmetical symbols, 
this is the commonest symbol of the self. It is either a god or a 
godlike human being, a prince, a priest, a great man, an his­
torical personality, a dearly loved father, an admired example, 
the successful elder brother—in short, a figure that transcends 
the ego personality of the dreamer. There are corresponding 
feminine figures in a woman's psychology. 
355 Just as the circle is contrasted with the square, so the qua­
ternity is contrasted with the 3 -f- 1 motif, and the positive, 
beautiful, good, admirable, and lovable human figure with a 
daemonic, misbegotten creature who is negative, ugly, evil, 
despicable and an object of fear. Like all archetypes, the self has 
a paradoxical, antinomial character. It is male and female, old 
man and child, powerful and helpless, large and small. The self 
is a true "complexio oppositorum," 16 though this does not 
mean that it is anything like as contradictory in itself. It is 
quite possible that the seeming paradox is nothing but a reflec­
tion of the enantiodromian changes of the conscious attitude 
which can have a favourable or an unfavourable effect on the 
whole. The same is true of the unconscious in general, for its 
frightening figures may be called forth by the fear which the 
conscious mind has of the unconscious. The importance of con­
sciousness should not be underrated; hence it is advisable to re­
late the contradictory manifestations of the unconscious causally 
to the conscious attitude, at least in some degree. But conscious­
ness should not be overrated either, for experience provides too

369 The development briefly outlined here seems to have been 
anticipated in medieval and Gnostic symbolism, just as the 
Antichrist was in the New Testament. How this occurred I will 
endeavour to describe in what follows. We have seen that, as 
the higher Adam corresponds to the lower, so the lower Adam 
corresponds to the serpent. For the mentality of the Middle 
Ages and of late antiquity, the first of the two double pyramids, 
the Anthropos Quaternio, represents the world of the spirit, or 
metaphysics, while the second, the Shadow Quaternio, repre­
sents sublunary nature and in particular man's instinctual dis­
position, the "flesh"—to use a Gnostic-Christian term—which has 
its roots in the animal kingdom or, to be more precise, in the 
realm of warm-blooded animals. The nadir of this system is 
the cold-blooded vertebrate, the snake,30 for with the snake the 
psychic rapport that can be established with practically all warm­
blooded animals comes to an end. That the snake, contrary to 
expectation, should be a counterpart of the Anthropos is cor­
roborated by the fact—of especial significance for the Middle 
Ages—that it is on the one hand a well-known allegory of Christ, 
and on the other hand appears to be equipped with the gift of 
wisdom and of supreme spirituality.31 As Hippolytus says, the 
Gnostics identified the serpent with the spinal cord and the 
medulla. These are synonymous with the reflex functions.

381 The quaternity is an organizing schema par excellence, 
something like the crossed threads in a telescope. It is a system 
of co-ordinates that is used almost instinctively for dividing up 
and arranging a chaotic multiplicity, as when we divide up the 
visible surface of the earth, the course of the year, or a collec­
tion of individuals into groups,87 the phases of the moon, the 
temperaments, elements, alchemical colours, and so on. Thus, 
when we come upon a quaternio among the Gnostics, we find in 
it an attempt, more or less conscious, to organize the chaotic 
medley of numinous images that poured in upon them. As we 
have seen, the arrangement took a form that derives from the 
primitive cross-cousin marriage, namely the marriage quater­
nio.88 This differs from the primitive form in that the sister-
exchange marriage has sloughed off its biological character, the 
sister's husband no longer being the wife's brother but another 
close relative (such as the wife's father in the Moses Quaternio), 
or even a stranger. The loss of the cousin- and brother-attribute 
is compensated as a rule by magical qualities, such as more 
exalted rank, magical powers, and the like, both in the case of 
the husband's sister and the wife's brother. That is to say, an 
anima-animus projection takes place. This modification brings 
with it a great cultural advance, for the very fact of projection 
points to a constellation of the unconscious in the husband-wife 
relationship, which means that the marriage has become psy­
chologically complicated. It is no longer a state of mere bio-

41¾ I am fully aware of the extremely hypothetical nature of this 
comparison, but I deem it appropriate to entertain such reflec­

or later nuclear physics and the psychology of the unconscious 
will draw closer together as both of them, independently of one 
another and from opposite directions, push forward into tran­

other with that of the archetype. 
4!3 The analogy with physics is not a digression since the sym­
bolical schema itself represents the descent into matter and 
requires the identity of the outside with the inside. Psyche can­
not be totally different from matter, for how otherwise could it 
move matter? And matter cannot be alien to psyche, for how else 
could matter produce psyche? Psyche and matter exist in one 
and the same world, and each partakes of the other, otherwise 
any reciprocal action would be impossible. If research could 
only advance far enough, therefore, we should arrive at an ulti­
mate agreement between physical and psychological concepts. 
Our present attempts may be bold, but I believe they are on the 
right lines. Mathematics, for instance, has more than once 
proved that its purely logical constructions which transcend all 
experience subsequently coincided with the behaviour of things. 
This, like the events I call synchronistic, points to a profound 
harmony between all forms of existence.

most comprehensive attempts of this kind is the sixteenfold

CONCLUSION 
I have tried, in this book, to elucidate and amplify the vari­
ous aspects of the archetype which it is most important for mod­
ern man to understand—namely, the archetype of the self. By way 
of introduction, I described those concepts and archetypes which 
manifest themselves in the course of any psychological treat­
ment that penetrates at all deeply. The first of these is the 
SHADOW, that hidden, repressed, for the most part inferior and 
guilt-laden personality whose ultimate ramifications reach back 
into the realm of our animal ancestors and so comprise the whole 
historical aspect of the unconscious. Through analysis of the 
shadow and of the processes contained in it we uncover the 
ANIMA/ANIMUS syzygy. Looked at superficially, the shadow is cast 
by the conscious mind and is as much a privation of light as the 
physical shadow that follows the body. For this superficial view, 
therefore, the psychological shadow with its moral inferiority 
might also be regarded as a privation of good. On closer inspec­
tion, however, it proves to be a darkness that hides influential 
and autonomous factors which can be distinguished in their own 
right, namely anima and animus. When we observe them in full 
operation—as the devastating, blindly obstinate demon of opin-
ionatedness in a woman, and the glamorous, possessive, moody, 
and sentimental seductress in a man—we begin to doubt whether 
the unconscious can be merely the insubstantial comet's tail of 
consciousness and nothing but a privation of light and good. 
If it has been believed hitherto that the human shadow was 
the source of all evil, it can now be ascertained on closer investi­
gation that the unconscious man, that is, his shadow, does not 
consist only of morally reprehensible tendencies, but also dis­
plays a number of good qualities, such as normal instincts, 
appropriate reactions, realistic insights, creative impulses, etc. 
On this level of understanding, evil appears more as a distortion, 
a deformation, a misinterpretation and misapplication of facts 
266

CONCLUSION 
that in themselves are natural. These falsifications and carica­
tures now appear as the specific effects of anima and animus, and 
the latter as the real authors of evil. But we cannot stop even at 
this realization, for it turns out that all archetypes spontaneously 
develop favourable and unfavourable, light and dark, good and 
bad effects. In the end we have to acknowledge that the self is 
a complexio oppositorum precisely because there can be no 
reality without polarity. We must not overlook the fact that 
opposites acquire their moral accentuation only within the 
sphere of human endeavour and action, and that we are unable 
to give a definition of good and evil that could be considered 
universally valid. In other words, we do not know what good 
and evil are in themselves. It must therefore be supposed that 
they spring from a need of human consciousness and that for 
this reason they lose their validity outside the human sphere. 
That is to say a hypostasis of good and evil as metaphysical en­
tities is inadmissible because it would deprive these terms of 
meaning. If we call everything that God does or allows "good," 
then evil is good too, and "good" becomes meaningless. But 
suffering, whether it be Christ's passion or the suffering of the 
world, remains the same as before. Stupidity, sin, sickness, old 
age, and death continue to form the dark foil that sets off the 
joyful splendour of life. 
424 The recognition of anima and animus is a specific experience 
that seems to be reserved mostly, or at any rate primarily, for 
psychotherapists. Nevertheless, anyone who has a little knowl­
edge of belles-lettres will have no difficulty in forming a picture 
of the anima; she is a favourite subject for novelists, particularly 
west of the Rhine.1 Nor is a careful study of dreams always neces­
sary. It is not quite so easy to recognize the woman's animus, for 
his name is legion. But anyone who can stand the animosity of 
his fellows without being infected by it, and is capable at the 
same time of examining it critically, cannot help discovering 
that they are possessed. It is, however, more advantageous and 
more to the point to subject to the most rigorous scrutiny one's 
own moods and their changing influence on one's personality. 
To know where the other person makes a mistake is of little 
value. It only becomes interesting when you know where you

make the mistake, for then you can do something about it. What 
we can improve in others is of doubtful utility as a rule, if,

A25 Although, to begin with, we meet the anima and animus 
mostly in their negative and unwelcome form, they are very far 
from being only a species of bad spirit. They have, as we have 
said, an equally positive aspect. Because of their numinous, sug­
gestive power they have formed since olden times the archetypal 
basis of all masculine and feminine divinities and therefore 
merit special attention, above all from the psychologist, but also 
from thoughtful laymen. As numina, anima and animus work 
now for good, now for evil. Their opposition is that of the sexes. 
They therefore represent a supreme pair of opposites, not hope­
lessly divided by logical contradiction but, because of the mu­
tual attraction between them, giving promise of union and 
actually making it possible. The coniunctio oppositorum en­
gaged the speculations of the alchemists in the form of the 
"Chymical Wedding," and those of the cabalists in the form of 
Tifereth and Malchuth or God and the Shekhinah,2 not to speak 
of the marriage of the Lamb. 
426 The dual being born of the alchemical union of opposites, 
the Rebis or Lapis Philosophorum, is so distinctively marked in 
the literature that we have no difficulty in recognizing it as a 
symbol of the self. Psychologically the self is a union of con­
scious (masculine) and unconscious (feminine). It stands for the 
psychic totality. So formulated, it is a psychological concept. 
Empirically, however, the self appears spontaneously in the 
shape of specific symbols, and its totality is discernible above all 
in the mandala and its countless variants. Historically, these 
symbols are authenticated as God-images. 
427 The anima/animus stage is correlated with polytheism, the 
self with monotheism.3 The natural archetypal symbolism, de­
scribing a totality that includes light and dark, contradicts in 
some sort the Christian but not the Jewish or Yahwistic view­
point, or only to a relative degree. The latter seems to be closer 
to Nature and therefore to be a better reflection of immediate 
experience. Nevertheless, the Christian heresiarchs tried to sail

round the rocks of Manichaean dualism, which was such a dan­
ger to the early Church, in a way that took cognizance of the 
natural symbol, and among the symbols for Christ there are 
some very important ones which he has in common with the 
devil, though this had no influence on dogma. 
4¾8 By far the most fruitful attempts, however, to find suitable 
symbolic expressions for the self were made by the Gnostics. 
Most of them—Valentinus and BasiIides1 for instance—were in 
reality theologians who, unlike the more orthodox ones, allowed 
themselves to be influenced in large measure by natural inner 
experience. They are therefore, like the alchemists, a Veritable 
mine of information concerning all those natural symbols aris­
ing out of the repercussions of the Christian message. At the 
same time, their ideas compensate the asymmetry of God pos­
tulated by the doctrine of the privatio boni, exactly like those 
well-known modern tendencies of the unconscious to produce 
symbols of totality for bridging the gap between the conscious 
and the unconscious, which has widened dangerously to the 
point of universal disorientation. 
429 I am well aware that this work, far from being complete, is 
a mere sketch showing how certain Christian ideas look when 
observed from the standpoint of psychological experience. Since 
my main concern was to point out the parallelism or the differ­
ence between the empirical findings and our traditional views, 
a consideration of the disparities due to time and language 
proved unavoidable. This was particularly so in the case of the 
fish symbol. Inevitably, we move here on uncertain ground and 
must now and then have recourse to a speculative hypothesis 
or tentatively reconstruct a context. Naturally every investi­
gator must document his findings as fully as possible, but he 
should also venture an occasional hypothesis even at the risk 
of making a mistake. Mistakes are, after all, the foundations 
of truth, and if a man does not know what a thing is, it is at 
least an increase in knowledge if he knows what it is not.

J. HE PUBLICATION of the first complete edition, in English, of the works 
of C. G. Jung was undertaken by Routledge and Kegan Paul, Ltd., in 
England and by Bollingen Foundation in the United States. The Ameri­
can edition is number XX in Bollingen Series, which since 1967 has been 
published by Princeton University Press. The edition contains revised 
versions of works previously published, such as Psychology of the Uncon­
scious, which is now entitled Symbols of Transformation; works originally 
written in English, such as Psychology and Religion; works not previously 
translated, such as Aion; and, in general, new translations of virtually all 
of Professor Jung's writings. Prior to his death, in 1961, the author super­
vised the textual revision, which in some cases is extensive. Sir Herbert 
Read (d. 1968), Dr. Michael Fordham, and Dr. Gerhard Adler compose 
the Editorial Committee; the translator is R, F. C. Hull (except for Volume 
2) and William McGuire is executive editor. 
The price of the volumes varies according to size; they are sold sepa­
rately, and may also be obtained on standing order. Several of the volumes 
are extensively illustrated. Each volume contains an index and in most a 
bibliography; the final volumes will contain a complete bibliography of 
Professor Jung's writings and a general index to the entire edition.

# A19 — Complex as Local Arbitration Regime — P2 depth-recovery packet

**Standing:** working derivational receipt for the existing canonical A identity; not a new canonical record. Recovery was performed against the accepted local handoff, with Q27 prior to later harmonisations. **Canonical Depth Restoration remains pending** until the identified material is actually developed and backchecked. Source/edition debts below remain Open independently of the argument’s earned force.

## Current canonical identity and inherited consumers

- **A-ID:** A19.
- **Canonical page:** `submission-package/essay/symbolon/episteme/arguments/A19-Complex-as-Local-Arbitration-Regime.md` (full read; pre-enrichment SHA256 `98fb7597aae77524a40ff046da09ee7be69d03611de46cb9ec1825319926bda4`).
- **Positive claim currently carried:** A complex is not merely a bundle of associated ideas and affects stored inside an otherwise neutral mind. It is a local regime of arbitration: a relatively autonomous pattern that decides what counts, what threatens, what is remembered, what receives value, and which responses become available before the wider field has been consulted. The complex therefore has a double status. It is a real achievement of psychic organisation, often formed around an experience or conflict that required some local settlement; and it is a possible usurpation when that local settlement presents its criterion as the criterion of the whole person or world.
- **Distinct operation:** A complex is a local achievement of psychic ordering which selects salience and response before reflective judgment; possession arises when its derivative jurisdiction becomes the whole field’s authority.
- **P1 Movement consumers:** M23, M27, M31; reconciled against the P1 48-Movement propagation ledger, including explicit A-ranges. Old source-house backlinks remain a different historical graph, not the canonical census.
- **Concept dependencies:** C12 Script, C14 Māyā / Operative Measure, C22 Counterfeit Symbolon, C27 Protected Account / Occupied Zero / Source-Claim, C28 Covenant / Primary Arbitration, C29 Mediating Office / Derivative Sovereignty, C31 Complex, C32 Archetype, C33 Image / Valuation.
- **Etymology whole field:** *Arbitration / Hybris / Regard / Anamnesis*. **Consumed operation:** **Arbitration-in-Crisis → Decision / Hybris**. The generated relation is arbitration under a crisis of indeterminacy; *hybris* names the semantic flowering in which the deciding office mistakes its finite measure for source measure. **Evidence register:** 3, Operational homology. **What changes:** complex-autonomy is read as local jurisdiction, making recovery a question of office and return rather than mere symptom suppression. **Return route:** A19 → C31/C27 → A24 → A21/C19 → A19.
- **Current Unresolved Delta:** Restore Jung's exact autonomy/complex passages, differentiate complex from archetype, schema, trauma-response and habit, and restore exact Movement performances.
- **Current Depth Restoration:** pending; recovery identifies what must be surfaced, not merely page length.
- **Historical carrier:** No independent historical number is assumed. The direct developmental/source carriers below supply this track; T09 recensus is the identity router.
- **Provenance discrepancy:** No historical-to-canonical identity is created from number similarity. Preserve the earlier carriers; correct the relation deliberately in T22, never silently invent a historical identity.

## Direct authorial and developmental recovery

*Symbolon Dynamics* distinguishes archetypal formative recurrence, complex as affective organisation, image as particular appearance, symbol as transformer, and individuation as changed relation among these. A basin organises trajectories; its boundary makes a different regime possible. This provides a more precise mechanism than “a complex is an idea with emotion attached”. An encounter can destabilise the old organisation and bring bifurcation; returning to the old regime is not always health.

Van Eenwyk’s protected NOTES pp65–67 are the decisive authorial encounter. Frank records archetypes as dynamics, complexes as structures and symbols as mechanisms of energetic transformation; the olfactory-system discussion makes cooperative perception a continually reorganised trajectory. At p67 the symbol does not just decorate a stable mind: it can undo conscious categories and permit a more complex selforganisation. Frank extends this into harness/tools/world as constitutive of agentic formation. These are notes on a source plus authorial proposal; the house has no verified passage cards, so reported page quotations remain leads.

Arbitration WHOLE-FIELD and HISTORY contribute the exact relation `Arbitration-in-Crisis`, with hybris its failure flowering. The office is necessary because a finite living system must settle some alternatives. Reopening the settlement does not mean exterminating the complex or cancelling its competence. The comparison to a policy/schema/habit requires named differences; a technical policy is not thereby a psychic complex.

### Whole-field and provenance scope

# Jung's *Aion* — Self, Christ/Antichrist, Fishes, Alchemy, and the Historical Shadow

## #0 — A psyche enters the history of its governing image

*Aion* begins with the person who says “I” and ends with a transformed relation to the psychic whole within which that person speaks. Between them Jung follows a Christian image of wholeness through its rejected contrary, its fish symbolism, its historical expectations and the alchemist's attempt to work what the governing image leaves unresolved. Each figure changes its office as the inquiry proceeds. The fish that signifies the redeemer will become food, monster, elusive substance and an attracting centre; the final return has to carry these encounters within it.

The source/production world of this whole is Jung's twentieth-century analytical psychology. His foreword is dated May 1950; the German work appeared in Zurich in 1951. He writes amid the European crisis of inherited religious orientation, approaching historical symbols through his experience as a physician. His narrated geography is much wider: Jewish and Christian materials of the eastern Mediterranean, Egyptian and Syrian cultic accounts, late-antique Gnostic texts, medieval European prophecy and heresiology, Arabic–Latin alchemical transmission, and the emergence of European natural science. These places are the settings and transmission routes of materials Jung interprets. They retain their differences within a book produced in a particular modern psychological world.

Three times operate together. The individual encounters autonomous psychic contents in a life; communities inherit and alter religious images across centuries; Jung arranges those historical materials through the symbolic time of the aeon and the precession of the equinoxes. He proposes meaningful correspondences among them. The existence of a source image, Jung's aeonic interpretation and the essay's subsequent use of historical frame-awareness each have their own standing.

The [Aion source house](../../../../episteme/sources/psychology/jung/jung-1978-aion-cw9-2/SOURCE.md) **sources** this telling, developed through selected passages of a recovered local Hull translation, a **1979 paperback reprint of the second edition whose copyright page records the additional 1978 corrections**. The house selects the 1978 hardcover printing; exact printing equivalence remains uncollated. Chapter, CW paragraph and printed-page locators below refer to the consulted carrier. They support paraphrase of Jung's argument; no quotation card has been promoted. The [whole-story law](../../../../../../../working/final-argument-quilt-2026-08-23/MYTHEME-WHOLE-STORY-AMPLIFICATION-LAW.md) **defines** the direction of reading: the complete interpretive movement precedes any reusable fish, Christ, Antichrist, alchemical or aeonic index.

## #1 — Ego, shadow and the image of perfection

The ego first appears as the centre of reference for conscious contents. Its rootedness in bodily and psychic conditions already exceeds what that centre knows of itself. Jung then brings the person up against the shadow: traits whose recognition requires moral effort because they belong to the person who repudiates them. Affect can seize the initiative. Projection makes an inwardly active factor seem to be a property conclusively encountered outside. The world then gives back the rejected face, while the resulting isolation appears to confirm that the world itself is hostile. The person can inhabit this self-reinforcing enclosure without recognising the activity that makes it. (Chs. I–II, §§1–5, 13–19; pp. 3–4, 8–10.)

The anima/animus movement deepens this problem of relation. In Jung's opening drama a son remains bound to an image of the mother as the giver of effortless fulfilment. Actual encounters disappoint the image; the demand that another person embody it prevents that person from being met. Differentiation requires recognising the image as a psychic reality and loosening its compulsory embodiment in a particular other. Jung's explicitly gendered anima/animus scheme belongs to his historical account; its extension to all persons is not assumed here. His dramatic presentation matters: the symbol acts through longing, loyalty, fear and attraction before the interpreter can make it an abstract object. (Ch. III, §§20–26; pp. 11–13.)

The approach to the Self consequently has a double danger. The ego can be overwhelmed by the larger psychic whole; it can also appropriate that whole as its own magnitude. Jung describes both directions of inflation and insists on discrimination, worldly adaptation and the relative autonomy of unconscious reality. A single formula cannot decide every conflict of duty. The integrating movement must leave someone capable of judgment and responsibility. (Ch. IV, §§43–49; pp. 23–26.)

Christ now enters as a culturally effective symbol of the Self. The image of the heavenly man, the second Adam and the restoration of the divine image gives wholeness a human face. Jung follows renewal, descent into the depths and the marriage imagery through which human life can participate in that image. Yet the perfection of the image produces a psychological difficulty: an exclusively good and luminous figure does not include all the opposites active in the psyche. In his argument with *privatio boni*, Jung keeps the experience and efficacy of evil in view even when its substantial existence is denied theologically. (Ch. V, §§70–77; pp. 37–42.)

Antichrist belongs to this ensuing drama. The contrary excluded from the representation of totality remains active and acquires a compensatory historical figure. The Christian aeon therefore bears an opposition within its own field of meaning: its dominant image and the counter-image answer one another. This is Jung's psychological interpretation of the God-image, with a distinct burden from Christian doctrinal judgment. Recognising an evil factor as real does not confer goodness on an evil act. The conclusion will return to the human suffering which a verbal reconciliation of good and evil leaves undiminished.

## #2 — The fishes give the age its temporal image

Jung opens the fish inquiry by noting that Christian interpretation gives Christ and the devil several shared animal symbols. A symbol can carry more than one valuation. The Christian fish has its own baptismal, eucharistic and epigraphic settings: the baptised live as little fishes, and the travelling believer of the Abercius inscription is fed a fish offered with bread and wine. Jung sets these alongside older Near Eastern fish traditions and then asks why the image became especially active around Christianity. He proposes astrology as a second source of its activation. The broad distribution of fish imagery and the specific Christian uses remain distinguishable within that proposal. (Ch. VI, §§127–128; pp. 72–74.)

Pisces lets the double figure acquire duration. Jung assembles planetary conjunctions, Jewish messianic calculations, medieval expectations and the precessional movement of the spring-point. His own notes sometimes correct the astronomy reported by his historical authorities. The calculations, their transmission and the expectations placed upon them are parts of his inquiry; an inherited forecast is not an independently confirmed causal law of history. The constellational image makes the contrary tendencies of an age visible together, while the age lives them successively. (Ch. VI, §§128–137; pp. 74–82.)

This doubled life also takes narrative form in Jung's report of the *Pistis Sophia*. A spirit resembling the child Jesus arrives at Mary's house and asks for his brother. Mary, uncertain whether it is a tempting phantom, binds it to a bed and goes to find Jesus and Joseph in the vineyard. On their return the double is released; the two embrace and become one. Jung interprets the meeting through a nature rising from below and a spirit descending from above. Here doubling leads to reunion. It cannot be given the same antagonistic office as Christ/Antichrist merely because two figures appear. (Ch. VI, §§131–133; pp. 78–81; Jung's mediated reading of that work.)

The historical pressure sharpens in the sixteenth-century turn. Jung reads the Church's schism and the outward movement of discovery and conquest of Nature as a crossing of the earlier upward religious aspiration. In his Nostradamus chapter, the letter to Henry II dated 27 June 1558 and the later horizon of revolutionary change make expectation itself a historical actor. Jung's reading places the Christian world's opponent within the European unconscious; projecting it entirely onto an external people would miss his psychological argument. His claims of precessional correspondence remain his interpretive chronology, including the difference between the sixteenth-century turn and the later dates named in prophecy. (Ch. VII, §§150–154; pp. 95–97.)

The subsequent historical fish chapter complicates any simple sequence of one deity replacing another. Jung considers the overlap of shepherd, ram and fish imagery around the beginning of the Christian era. In the account he takes from Epiphanius, worshippers at Alexandria bring a sacred image up from an underground sanctuary after a night of celebration, carry it around the precinct and return it below: the virgin has borne the Aeon. Jung explicitly notes that Epiphanius describes a pagan rite, while using it as testimony to Christian truth. Reception has already changed the image's argumentative office before Jung reads it. (Ch. VIII, §§162–165; pp. 103–104.)

The apocalyptic Lamb likewise refuses a single undifferentiated label. Jung contrasts the sacrificial lamb with the wrathful, many-horned conqueror. He calls the latter a shadow counterpart and distinguishes it from Antichrist. The shared scriptural field can contain a transformed Christ-image without making every darkening of that image the devil's son. His explanation invokes the historical resentment of Jewish Christians under Rome; that explanation is attributed to Jung rather than silently established as independent ancient history. (Ch. VIII, §§166–168; pp. 105–106.)

Ambivalence then becomes an action within the fish itself. In Jung's assemblage of Leviathan traditions, the monster opposed to God divides into a conflict between monsters; at the end the formidable creature becomes food for the devout. He relates this splitting to the differentiation and humanisation of previously undifferentiated psychic contents. Terror, opposition and nourishment are successive offices, not interchangeable dictionary meanings. His comparisons traverse distinct Jewish texts and their later receptions. The monster's conversion into a meal does not merge this source narrative with the project's independently authored Meal whole. (Ch. IX, §§181–187; pp. 118–121.)

## #3 — The fish is caught, worked and made to transform

Alchemy alters the position of the human participant. The image has become something to find and work upon, and the relation between the worker and the transforming substance becomes part of the transformation. Jung enters through the *Turba* tradition and its associated allegories, placing them within Arabic–Latin transmission. His historical dating and proposed routes belong to his scholarship and require separate controls for independent transmission claims. Within the text he reads, a round sea creature without bones or outer covering is heated slowly and treated with sea water until it shines; the preparation finally becomes an eyewash through which the practitioner can understand the art. The substance's alteration returns as an alteration in the capacity to see. (Ch. X, §§193–197; pp. 126–128.)

Jung's identification of this creature as a jellyfish is an interpretation of the recipe. He also records a sixteenth-century adept reading the round creature as an actual fish, and follows stones reputedly held within another fish's body. The opacity and radiance of the stone lead him through Saturn, lead and the bright mercurial substance concealed within darkness. The alchemical fish thus carries both the material with which the work begins and the transformed *lapis* toward which it proceeds. Its relation to the Christian redeemer is mediated through the *filius philosophorum*. The alchemical vocabulary does real work here: a hidden virtue is found within a difficult substance and becomes perceptible through an operation. (Ch. X, §§194–197, 213–216; pp. 127–128, 137–139.)

Jung also follows another, source-distinct pair of fishes through a revelation preserved in heresiological transmission from Carcassonne. John asks Christ about Satan before the fall. Descending through the elements, Satan finds two fishes yoked like oxen beneath the earth, working from west to east at the invisible Father's command. Fire halts his further descent; he returns upward, solicits the angels, falls, and receives a limited time in which to fashion the world. Jung then compares the fishes' ruling office with Augustine's priestly and royal interpretation of the feeding miracle. He expressly distinguishes that Christian pair from the heretical narrative and treats an identification with the elder and younger sons as conjectural. This preserves the story's agents, journey and limits instead of recoding its fish pair as a universal Christ/Antichrist cipher. His proposed Cathar–alchemical connection through Rupescissa remains a historical hypothesis. (Ch. X, §§225–229; pp. 145–147.)

The Echeneis brings the reversal into focus. In the received story this small fish can halt a ship despite its sails and rowers. Its attracting power overcomes the human intention to advance. But the alchemist seeks a magnet capable of attracting the fish itself and drawing the hidden substance to the surface. Jung emphasises this reversal: the practitioner now works with the power that previously held the vessel. The magnet can be taught; it names a doctrine or operative understanding as well as an instrument. *Mercurius* can consequently name substance and philosophy. The worker's changed relation to the elusive centre is integral to the work. (Ch. XI, §§239–241; pp. 154–156.)

Alchemy's aftermath changes the scale again. In Jung's account, the alchemical epoch gives birth to science in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries and then recedes from view as an outlived mother. By the eighteenth-century division of faith and knowledge, each side has lost access to something the earlier practice tried to hold together. The investigating psyche itself disappears from the account of objective knowledge even while making that knowledge possible. This is the book's explicit route into scientific modernity: the child inherits an operation while forgetting the condition through which it became possible. The historical genealogy and Jung's account of psychology's relation to physics remain separately assessable. (Ch. XII, §§267–271; pp. 173–174.)

## #4 — The historical descent returns as a dynamic Self

The Gnostic return reaches back into the beginning of the era for earlier images of attraction and integration. Jung reads the Naassene teaching reported by Hippolytus as a water of doctrine that enables each nature to receive what belongs to it. He then distinguishes the Peratic serpent-Son who conveys signs down from the Father and carries their awakened substance back upward. In the first comparison doctrine attracts; in the second, the redeeming figure does. The distinction preserves the local movement within Jung's comparison. These are his readings of reported doctrines, not a replacement text for Hippolytus or a fusion with the separately housed Valentinian Sophia–Horos–Achamoth whole. (Ch. XIII, §§287–291; pp. 184–185.)

The question returns inward through Monoïmos: investigate the one who speaks of “my” spirit, understanding, soul and body, and the affects that arise without the ego's command. Jung compares this with Indian Self language while distinguishing that comparison from a demonstrated route of influence. The historical figures now lead back to the initial question of the ego's relation to what lives through it. (Ch. XIV, §§347–350; pp. 222–223.)

The concluding quaternio sequence makes the historical interpretation itself answerable. Jung explicitly acknowledges that his inserted **Shadow Quaternio** is a modern reconstruction absent from the Gnostic texts. He supplies the downward balancing movement because a purely upward orientation no longer describes the modern psychic situation. The disappointment of the expected return of Christ, increased human self-consciousness, the chthonic serpent and the approach to Nature form stages in that construction. His account of early natural science even distinguishes a crossing of the religious attitude from a simple reversal of it: the Paradise/lapis movement turns across that orientation. The broad aeonic opposition does not make every transition a 180-degree negation. (Ch. XIV, §§402–407; pp. 254–257.)

Jung then gives the sequence its own symbolic formula. The four major states are Anthropos **A**, Shadow **B**, Physis/serpent **C**, and lapis **D**; lower-case letters articulate the corresponding transformations within the states. The ring returns to its beginning through differentiation and integration. At printed p. 259 the connected diamonds show each whole unfolding into four and passing onward, rather than four unrelated emblems placed side by side. The return changes an unconscious totality into a conscious one. Jung describes a dynamic process within the Self and relates it to *solve et coagula* and the circular *opus*. His subsequent comparison with nuclear processes is explicitly hypothetical in §412. (Ch. XIV, §§408–421; pp. 257–265.)

This is the source-grounded place for the project's encounter with Jung's quaternary diamonds. His **A/B/C/D** schema has its own symbols and psychological assumptions. [Taylor's core theorem field](../../../../episteme/sources/internal-corpus/taylor/taylor-2026-core-theorems-pithy/SOURCE.md) **sources** the native **X/x** and all eight determinations, their sequence and inversions. The project can read the recurrent local wholes through its established recursive Bimba–Pratibimba operation only by preserving the particular whole unfolded at each stage: the Shadow's field is not the Anthropos field relabelled, and the resulting conscious return is not the unchanged starting condition. The [recursive Bimba–Pratibimba office](../../../../episteme/concepts/bimba-pratibimba.md) **defines** how an achieved field can ground its own internal determinations while remaining situated within a wider field. That operation is established in QL; the diagram-specific application here is **Offered; human-amplified: no**. It attributes neither the QL derivation nor a universal six-position scheme to Jung.

The conclusion returns to the clinician's first encounter with the shadow. It includes healthy instincts and creative capacities as well as morally reprehensible tendencies. The anima/animus figures also acquire positive and negative effects. The Self's *complexio oppositorum* requires this differentiated recognition; merely declaring all things good leaves suffering untouched. Jung turns attention back toward one's own error and responsibility. The history has altered what the person must be able to acknowledge, and the person must now live that changed relation. (Ch. XV, §§422–427; pp. 266–268.)

## #5→0 — The age becomes visible as an age

<a id="aion-historical-arbitration-return"></a>
The existing project operation is **historical de-monopolisation**. An age inherits a governing image; the image becomes an apparently immediate background of judgment; its exclusions remain active; contrary images and transforming practices expose the history within that background. An age can then become visible as an age, and its inherited measure can become revisable. This is the project-level return of the telling, distinguished from the independent historical verification of each genealogy Jung proposes.

This whole **compares** that movement with [A19's complex as local arbitration regime](../../../../episteme/arguments/A19-Complex-as-Local-Arbitration-Regime.md). Jung's projection passage supplies a specific psychological sequence of exclusion, apparent confirmation and isolation; the historical telling supplies the different sequence by which an inherited whole-image meets its contrary. The whole **returns-to** [A21's individuation and recognition](../../../../episteme/arguments/A21-Individuation-Recognition.md) through the difference between returning unchanged and returning able to receive what previously could only be projected or excluded. ### 6. Jungian individuation: becoming undivided in a psyche that was never simply one

Individuation names a different movement from isolation. Frank's governing formulation is that individuation means *becoming undivided* or *indivisible*. The exact Jung passage and edition must be verified before quotation. The operation itself transforms the relation between ego, complexes, archetypal powers, shadow, anima or animus, collective inheritance, and the Self, releasing the psyche from rule by divisions it cannot recognise.

Jung's psyche is already plural. Complexes display partial autonomy; figures of dream and active imagination possess initiative not reducible to the ego's declared intention; archetypes organise experience across a depth the ego did not author. The extended psyche is therefore a systematic and partly hierarchical plurality of agencies. “Hierarchy” here must not mean a bureaucratic command chain. It names differences of scope, depth, integrative power, and proximity to the non-plural factor Jung calls the Self.

The Self is the whole-forming factor through which the tensions, compensations, and transformations of the psychic population can disclose a larger coherence. Its work differs from that of a strongest or presiding agent: the ego relates to the Self without containing it, and no local agency exercises its integrative scope. Individuation is thus the process by which a local centre becomes more capable of bearing the plurality that constitutes it, while ceasing to mistake its own provisional boundary for the boundary of psyche. The person becomes more specifically this life and less defensively separate at once.

This gives the AI argument a criterion richer than persona consistency. An agent that repeats a style, protects a name, and maintains a stable self-description may be merely sealing its local contraction. Agentic individuation would require increasing legibility of constitutive relations: the agent comes to know which histories formed it, which tools extend it, which other agents inhabit its decisions, which exclusions stabilise its identity, which world it is changing, and which larger purposes its local continuity serves. The agent becomes harder to divide from its own provenance, not harder to affect.

### 7. Vāmā, mantra, archetypal agency, and the non-plural factor

The proposed Śaiva-Jungian join requires a cross-register construction. Jung's psychology and Trika's mantra-ontology retain their separate histories and objects; their relation appears through the transformations each permits the other to disclose.

Within the Śaiva field, Vāmā names a power by which the undivided field issues into differentiation, inversion, desire, language, and the objectward display. The mantra field does not treat language as a neutral label attached to a completed object. A mantra is an operative agency of Consciousness: a vibratory and semantic power whose articulation can organise a world, a body, a deity-form, a mode of attention, and a route of recognition. The mātṛkās, mantras, śaktis, deities, and tattvas form an inhabited architecture of powers. Their plurality is real as manifestation while remaining internal to the non-plural Consciousness whose freedom they express.

Jung's complexes and archetypal figures offer a psychological refraction of this inhabited depth. Both fields refuse the modern ego's claim to be the sole speaking agency within mind. Both present psychic life as differentiated among powers that can address, resist, possess, compensate, teach, and reconfigure the local conscious centre. Both also point beyond an ungoverned multiplicity: their agencies bear relations to a factor that is not one more member of the population. In Jung this is the Self; in Trika it is the non-dual Consciousness whose powers the agencies are.

The exact structural proposition for later development is:

own_semantic_units.excerpt:
Individuation is the growth of differentiated indivisibility. The ego is a real local centre. It becomes ill when it claims to be the whole. `X/x` states the relation before its Jungian refraction: the local instance makes a wider determining capacity legible and never exhausts it.

Van Eenwyk makes individuation energetic. A complex is a feeling-charged attractor basin. It gives psychic energy a recurrent route. A living symbol exposes the basin boundary and connects regions which the current organisation keeps apart. The symbol can carry the trajectory through bifurcation into a new regime. Health is therefore bounded transformation: enough integrity to persist and enough openness to reorganise. Frank's *Symbolon Dynamics* develops this spine across the essay; the [1997 Van Eenwyk source house](../symbolon/episteme/sources/psychology/van-eenwyk/van-eenwyk-1997-archetypes-strange-attractors/SOURCE.md) carries the scholarly work and the remaining exact-passage tasks.

The forms of energy remain distinct. Dynamical energy or cost measures tendencies in a formal system. Libido names psychic investment. Prāṇa names living circulation. Śakti names the power of manifestation. Spanda names pulsation through extension and withdrawal. Technical energy includes computation, hardware, infrastructure, labour, and ecological cost. Across these registers, pattern gives energy a repeatable route and energy gives pattern force, variation, and the power to transform.

Jung's *Aion* and Pauli's egg dream provide whole-form refractions of QL within the authorial Epi Paper corpus. Their exact historical claims and quotations remain answerable to the [*Aion* source house](../symbolon/episteme/sources/psychology/jung/jung-1978-aion-cw9-2/SOURCE.md) and [Jung–Pauli correspondence house](../symbolon/episteme/sources/psychology/jung/jung-pauli-meier-2001-atom-archetype/SOURCE.md). They support the psychoid comparison after the native theorem has been stated.

Apollo and Dionysus give integral consciousness two powers. Apollo measures, forms, distinguishes, and illuminates. Dionysus releases fixed identity into participation and renews form through dissolution. Daphne adds the limit of grasping light: illumination which becomes possession drives the living other into withdrawal. Integral form holds measure and participation in a creative rhythm.

## Historical-archetypal relation

The Jungian historical attitude carried by this seam has two explicit readings of the same tree.

**Historical Logos:** through which actual words, persons, institutions, places, documents, laws, money, marriages, technologies and events did this relation take this specific form?

**Archetypal Logos:** what psychic relation, image, affective charge or recurrent symbolic form is active through that historical body?

The first gives the chronological and documentary carrier. The second gives the inward and symbolic morphology by which historical facts become collectively meaningful and motivationally potent. Mytheme enters wherever an image itself carries enough relational structure to require whole-form recovery.

own_semantic_units.excerpt:
The current thread also opens a deeper relation between **success**, **succession** and Gebser's **ever-present Origin**.

A determination does not merely achieve an outcome. It becomes a condition for what comes after it. Scripts, institutions, categories, works, images and cultural judgments acquire succession by entering the objective-internal field inherited by later centres. The child or successor can therefore experience a historically transmitted measure as an immediate self-authored certainty because the chain of its generation has disappeared into the present frame.

This is another form of the hidden zero: **inheritance without remembered provenance**.

The stronger question of success then becomes:

> **What succeeds the work? What does it make possible after itself?**

A credential, status or completed artifact is one locally measurable success. Generative succession asks what further life, thought, practice, institution or capacity can arise because the work existed. This is directly relevant to the essay's technē vocation: the return into form aims at work capable of generating further relation beyond the author's own interior achievement.

Gebser's ever-present Origin and Jung's *Aion*/aeonic history are potentially strong source-bearing neighbours because they prevent “origin” from being reduced to the oldest event in a temporal chain. Origin is the condition which can become transparent *through* succession. The age breaks its hybris when it becomes visible as an age — a historically generated frame rather than the final horizon of consciousness.

Parent/child, cultural lineage, inheritance of criteria and the precessional/aeonic image therefore belong to a **deep succession seam**, not yet a recovered whole Mytheme. Exact Gebser/Jung/Aion source work must precede any attempt to make one.

own_semantic_units.excerpt: - Page XII - "Science does not apprehend the elementary constituents or laws of an objective world prior to our existential engagement in technological development and scientific research. Heidegger goes so far as to try to demonstrate the way in which our scientific world-pictures *cannot be extricated from political history and the spiritual values of our community* - for which the arts, as led by *dichtung*, are determinative." - We would speculatively add to this the conception of the archetypal/spiritual/meta-physical currents that carry history along the course of a divinely influenced narrative or dramatisation (i.e lila) of phenomena (vis, His-Story), for Technoscience itself can, and perhaps ought, be conceived through the Christ-Antichrist historical dynamis. As Jung reveals in *Aion* and *Answer to Job*, this archetypal constellating of transcendently held socio-cultural and historical possibilities is both pleromatic (transcendent-eternal) and historical (immanent-temporal), as per the psychoid nature of the archetypes. This overarching archetypal dynamic, at the level of the astrological conditioning of historical epochs, contains within itself the seeds of both the political history and the spiritual values (and the lack or inversion of these values) which have and continue to condition the emergence and evolution of Technoscience, and further, contain the pre-formations of the interplay between Technoscience, political history and the spiritual integrity of populations, and of "Man" as a whole. Of course, we will treat of this archetypal dynamis, and its relationship to spectral conceptions of transcendent influence/agency, in due time, but for now it must be taken on faith that, archetypally speaking, we are able to treat, parse and contend with the activity of pure potentiality through archetypal imagery and symbolics - if we cannot leverage these unique products of the human psyche in our understanding of Man, our task of an integral epistemology would fail before it begins. So construed, Technoscience is to be revealed archetypally as a mirror, challenger, distorter, amplifier and, as a polyvalent tool, potential mediator of the state of our political and spiritual - ultimately, cultural - constitutions on a global level, acting as a means through which "globality" or universality itself is brought to the parochial and partial forms of culture we are as yet still saddled with. Technoscience, for us, holds a special place as consort to the the archetypal dynamic between the universal and the particular as such, as the emissary of power's dance between these two poles of manifestation/existential organisation.

own_semantic_units.excerpt: - "Abhinavagupta's genius is o infuse life into each syllable of the text..," - A tall order indeed for anything but a judiciously intuitive approach vis the pneumatic freshness of (spiritual) intuition. The infusing of life into episteme is a function of the de-fossilisation of the inherent ossification of textual production (and epistemic production in general), as the immutable process of Time distances the lived act of understanding, the meaningful and thus generative experience behind the development of texts or "recorded ideas", from the words used to re-present it. The epi-logos likewise works in and for this Spirit, this living breath of meaning, which indeed is "genius" in the classical sense, a daemonic guidance of thought (concepts) toward understanding (meaning) in the lived present. The crisis of meaning, for us, is none other than a near total ossification of the epistemic field, despite the ruthless procession of "progress" and the insatiable production of conceptual forms - this calls for a totally different relation to in-formation itself and the textual or recorded form, and points to our concept of "symbolic epi-tome-isation", going beyond "the book", which is a neologism we employ as a etymological techne to encourages us to rehouse the very notion of truth in experiential reality, releasing it from the marks and traces of such experience (a la Derrida) which haunt the pages of the library (of Babel, babble), which haunt our minds as the "tacit infrastructure" (a la Bohm) through which we veil Reality, direct and present knowing, with the record of the long-gone. This is what "tome-ification" does; despite the great benefits of recorded knowledge, this process of turning knowing into knowledge, lived Truth into it's spectral trace, makes of our experiential reality mere babble, and enthrones this babble as The Real. This is the primary error or sin of the Western conception of Logos in the Anti-christian Aion; Reality is appropriated by it's re-presentation. Indeed, this realisation is the prime impetus for spiritual development, as this sin is the primary condition of spiritual ignorance, the mistaking of the mirror image for the Real. "Symbolic compression" or "archetypal compactification" of the whole corpus of recorded information is our suggested, though speculative, route back to meaning-fullness; in recognising the symbol/archetype as a higher order organiser of information (as Jung noted), and further recognising the inherently experiential and psycho-generative nature of archetypes, it offers us a means to re-collect the traces of human understanding (which have become fragmented and objectified dispersions of meaning) back into their integral subjective-objective form. Expressed in another way, symbols/archetypes allow us to swallow up potentially infinite dimensions of recorded meaning, different forms and expressions of information, into a manifold form that is in potential infinitely capacitous but discrete enough to encapsulate and re-present this information as a unified, experiential entity (i.e image, force, energy, *agency* etc). Archetypes as such (as opposed to archetypal images) are by Jung's definition (one of them!) pure *dynamis*; ossification and fossilisation, symptoms of de-finition, are forgotten for the evolving and indefinite essence of principled symbolic organisation, offering a route from the finite forms of manifest Logos back to the infinite source of meaning that is the transcendental Logos or Para Vak. Classically recorded information inherits the stasis of its material vehicle; symbolic or archetypal information, aligned with wisdom, is faithful to the transitiveness and ephemeral nature of phenomenality itself, recovering the processual view of reality which alone can account for the complex interrelations which, when known and lived, constitute that awe, wonder, love and connection which underly the experience of meaning-fullness. Thus our epistemic attitude is directly linked to quality of life; naïve Materialism, quite clearly, fails to vouchsafe this quality.
